Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 sit inside the Section 5 argument (so the hierarchy nests them in PP8) but the paper announces them for use 'both here and in the next two sections'; the edges from them into Sections 6 and 7 are real and kept.

Section 3's plan before 'The contrapositive formulation' is a heuristic outline of the proof; rather than one proof-sketch node (which would swallow the definitions of k, the copies and the candidate pairs) its informal estimates were emitted as claims/remarks with rigor heuristic or semi_formal, and the definitions as their own nodes.

nodes.name: Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture (Marton's conjecture)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $A \subset \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a set with $|A + A| \leqslant K|A|$. Then $A$ is covered by at most $2 K^{C}$ cosets\footnote{The factor of $2$ is needed to deal with the case where $K$ is close to $1$. If $H_0$ is a subgroup of $\mathbf{F}_2^n$ and $A \subseteq H_0$ is a subset of size $(1-\varepsilon)|H_0|$ for some small $\varepsilon>0$, then in order to obtain the bound $|H|\leqslant|A|$, we need to pick a subgroup $H$ of $H_0$ of index 2 and cover $A$ by the two cosets of that subgroup.} of some subgroup $H \leqslant \mathbf{F}_2^n$ of size at most $|A|$.
nodes.statement_short: A set $A\subset\mathbf{F}_2^n$ with doubling $K$ is covered by $2K^C$ cosets of a subgroup of size at most $|A|$.
assumptions: $A \subset \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a set with $|A + A| \leqslant K|A|$
conclusions: $A$ is covered by at most $2 K^{C}$ cosets\footnote{The factor of $2$ is needed to deal with the case where $K$ is close to $1$. If $H_0$ is a subgroup of $\mathbf{F}_2^n$ and $A \subseteq H_0$ is a subset of size $(1-\varepsilon)|H_0|$ for some small $\varepsilon>0$, then in order to obtain the bound $|H|\leqslant|A|$, we need to pick a subgroup $H$ of $H_0$ of index 2 and cover $A$ by the two cosets of that subgroup.} of some subgroup $H \leqslant \mathbf{F}_2^n$ of size at most $|A|$
nodes.label: pfr-conj

nodes.name: Covering by few cosets implies small doubling
nodes.statement: Note that if $A$ is covered by at most $r$ cosets of a subgroup $H$ of size at most $|A|$, then $|A+A|\leqslant (\binom r2+1)|A|$, so \Cref{pfr-conj} allows one to pass from the property of having a small doubling constant to the property of being contained in a small union of cosets of a subgroup of size at most $|A|$ and back again with at most a polynomial loss in the parameters.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, a set covered by $r$ cosets of a subgroup of size at most $|A|$ has doubling at most $\binom r2+1$.

nodes.name: Ruzsa's bound for Marton's conjecture
nodes.statement: The first result in this direction was due to Imre Ruzsa~\cite{ruzsa-fin-field}, who obtained an upper bound of $2K^2 2^{K^4}$ in place of the desired $2K^C$.
nodes.statement_short: Ruzsa: covering by $2K^2 2^{K^4}$ cosets.

nodes.name: Sanders' quasi-polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa bound
nodes.statement: Sanders~\cite{sanders} made a dramatic breakthrough by proving the first bounds of shape $\ll \exp(\log^{C_1} K)$, showing that $C_1 = 4 + \varepsilon$ is permissible here.
nodes.statement_short: Sanders: bounds of shape $\exp(\log^{4+\varepsilon} K)$.

nodes.name: Konyagin's refinement of Sanders' bound
nodes.statement: A variant of Sanders' argument due to Konyagin (not published by Konyagin, but described by Sanders in~\cite{sanders2}, and see also the comments on page 8 of~\cite{gmt}) showed that $C_1 = 3 + \varepsilon$ is permissible.
nodes.statement_short: Konyagin: exponent $3+\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Green-Tao: PFR for downsets
nodes.statement: We also remark that \Cref{pfr-conj} (with worse values of $C$) was previously established in the special case when $A$ was a downset in~\cite{gt-freiman}.
nodes.statement_short: The conjecture, with worse constants, holds for downsets.

nodes.name: Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa theorem in characteristic 2 (C = 12)
nodes.statement: \Cref{pfr-conj} is true with $C = 12$.
nodes.statement_short: Marton's conjecture holds with $C=12$.
conclusions: \Cref{pfr-conj} is true with $C = 12$.
nodes.label: pfr

nodes.name: Liao's improvement to C = 11
nodes.statement: Since the initial release of this preprint, Jyun-Jie Liao has given a refinement of the argument that improves the constant $C=12$ in \Cref{pfr} to $C=11$ (with corresponding numerical improvements to our other main results and applications); see~\cite{liao1,liao2}.
nodes.statement_short: Liao refines the argument to get $C=11$.

nodes.name: Deduction of weak PFR over Z (via Green-Manners-Tao)
nodes.statement: It was shown in~\cite[Theorem 1.11]{gmt} that \Cref{pfr-entropy} (or \Cref{pfr}) in characteristic $2$ implies the so-called `weak' polynomial Freiman--Ruzsa conjecture over $\mathbf{Z}$, so that is now a theorem as well.
nodes.statement_short: Cite [GMT, Thm 1.11]: entropic PFR in characteristic 2 implies weak PFR over $\mathbf{Z}$.

nodes.name: Weak polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa theorem over Z
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a finite subset of $\mathbf{Z}^D$ for some $D$, and suppose that $|A+A| \leqslant K|A|$. Then there is some set $A' \subseteq A$, $|A'| \geqslant K^{-C_1/2} |A|$, with $\dim A' \leqslant C_2 \log K$, for some absolute\footnote{If one traces through the arguments in~\cite{gmt} (dropping all terms involving the exponent $1-1/C_{\mathrm{PFR}}$, and using the constant $C=11$ from \Cref{pfr-entropy} below), one finds that one can take $C_1 = 20C = 220$ and $C_2 = \frac{40}{\log 2}$. The reason we have stated \Cref{th13} with a $C_1/2$ in the exponent is so that the constants $C_1, C_2$ here are the same as the ones in~\cite{gmt}.} constants $C_1,C_2>0$.
nodes.statement_short: A set in $\mathbf{Z}^D$ with doubling $K$ has a $K^{-O(1)}$-dense subset of dimension $O(\log K)$.
assumptions: $A$ be a finite subset of $\mathbf{Z}^D$ for some $D$
$|A+A| \leqslant K|A|$
conclusions: there is some set $A' \subseteq A$, $|A'| \geqslant K^{-C_1/2} |A|$, with $\dim A' \leqslant C_2 \log K$
nodes.label: th13

nodes.name: Strong PFR conjecture over Z
nodes.statement: We remark that there is also a `strong' PFR conjecture over $\mathbf{Z}$ (though its formulation requires care; see~\cite{lovett-regev} and~\cite{manners-pfr-formulation} for more discussion). This remains a challenging open problem.
nodes.statement_short: The strong PFR conjecture over $\mathbf{Z}$ (with a careful formulation) remains open.

nodes.name: Additive stability (approximate homomorphisms) in F_2^n
nodes.statement: There is a constant $C_3$ such that if $f: \mathbf{F}_2^m \to \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a function such that the set $\{ f(x)+f(y)-f(x+y): x,y \in \mathbf{F}_2^m\}$ has cardinality at most $K$, then $f$ may be written as $g+h$, where $g$ is linear and the range of $h$ is a set of cardinality $O(K^{C_3})$.
nodes.statement_short: A map with few additive defects is linear plus a map of polynomially small range.
assumptions: $f: \mathbf{F}_2^m \to \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a function such that the set $\{ f(x)+f(y)-f(x+y): x,y \in \mathbf{F}_2^m\}$ has cardinality at most $K$
conclusions: $f$ may be written as $g+h$, where $g$ is linear and the range of $h$ is a set of cardinality $O(K^{C_3})$
nodes.label: additive-stability

nodes.name: Ruzsa's equivalence (proof of Corollary 1.4)
nodes.statement: The equivalence of this and \Cref{pfr} is due to Ruzsa~\cite[Conjecture 2.2.3]{ruzsa-sumsets-survey}. Ruzsa did not publish the proof, but he communicated it to the second author and the details may be found in~\cite{green-pfr-note}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Ruzsa's (unpublished, written up by Green) equivalence of Corollary 1.4 with Theorem 1.2.

nodes.name: Big-O notation
nodes.statement: Here, as usual, $O(X)$ denotes a quantity bounded by $CX$ for some absolute constant~$C$.

nodes.name: Polynomial linearity testing in F_2^n
nodes.statement: There is a constant $C_4$ with the following property. Suppose that $f : \mathbf{F}_2^m \to \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a function such that, if $x, y$ are selected uniformly at random from $\mathbf{F}_2^m$, $\mathbf{P}(f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)) \geqslant 1/K$. Then there is a homomorphism $g \colon \mathbf{F}_2^m \to \mathbf{F}_2^n$ such that $\mathbf{P}(f(x) = g(x)) \gg K^{-C_4}$.
nodes.statement_short: A map that is additive with probability $1/K$ agrees with a homomorphism on a $K^{-O(1)}$ fraction.
assumptions: $f : \mathbf{F}_2^m \to \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a function such that, if $x, y$ are selected uniformly at random from $\mathbf{F}_2^m$, $\mathbf{P}(f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y)) \geqslant 1/K$
conclusions: there is a homomorphism $g \colon \mathbf{F}_2^m \to \mathbf{F}_2^n$ such that $\mathbf{P}(f(x) = g(x)) \gg K^{-C_4}$
nodes.label: partial-additivity

nodes.name: Pointer to Samorodnitsky (proof of Corollary 1.5)
nodes.statement: See~\cite[Theorem 4.1]{samorodnitsky}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from PFR by Samorodnitsky's Theorem 4.1.

nodes.name: Notation X >> Y
nodes.statement: The notation $X\gg Y$ means that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $X\geqslant cY$.

nodes.name: Polynomial inverse theorem for the U^3(F_2^n) norm
nodes.statement: There is a constant $C_5$ with the following property. Let $f \colon \mathbf{F}_2^n \to \mathbf{C}$ be a $1$-bounded function such that $\|f\|_{U^3(\mathbf{F}_2^n)} \geqslant 1/K$. Then there exists a quadratic polynomial $P \colon \mathbf{F}_2^n \to \mathbf{F}_2$ such that \[ |\frac{1}{2^n} \sum_{x \in \mathbf{F}_2^n} f(x) (-1)^{P(x)}| \gg K^{-C_5}.\]
nodes.statement_short: A 1-bounded $f$ with $\|f\|_{U^3}\ge 1/K$ correlates polynomially with a quadratic phase.
assumptions: $f \colon \mathbf{F}_2^n \to \mathbf{C}$ be a $1$-bounded function such that $\|f\|_{U^3(\mathbf{F}_2^n)} \geqslant 1/K$
conclusions: there exists a quadratic polynomial $P \colon \mathbf{F}_2^n \to \mathbf{F}_2$ such that \[ |\frac{1}{2^n} \sum_{x \in \mathbf{F}_2^n} f(x) (-1)^{P(x)}| \gg K^{-C_5}.\]
nodes.label: u3-inverse

nodes.name: Mudgal's sum-product theorem for iterated sumsets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subset \mathbf{R}$ be a finite set with at least two elements. Then either then $m$-fold sumset $mA$ or the $m$-fold product set $A^{(m)}$ has cardinality at least $|A|^{f(m)}$, where $f(m) \rightarrow \infty$ as $m \rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: For finite $A\subset\mathbf{R}$, $|mA|$ or $|A^{(m)}|$ is at least $|A|^{f(m)}$ with $f(m)\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Bourgain-Chang theorem
nodes.statement: This generalizes a well-known result of Bourgain and Chang~\cite{bourgain-chang}, who established this when $A$ is a set of integers.
nodes.statement_short: The integer case of Corollary 1.7.

nodes.name: Entropic Ruzsa distance
nodes.statement: If $X, Y$ are two finitely supported random variables taking values in an additive group $G$, then we define \begin{equation} \dist{X}{Y} \coloneqq \ent{X' - Y'} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{X'} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Y'}, \end{equation} where $X', Y'$ are independent copies of $X, Y$.
nodes.origin_citation: Ruzsa 2009; Tao 2010 (Sumset and inverse sumset theory for Shannon entropy); Green, Manners & Tao 2023 (Sumsets and entropy revisited)
nodes.statement_short: $d[X;Y]=H[X'-Y']-\frac12H[X']-\frac12H[Y']$ for independent copies $X',Y'$.

nodes.name: Ruzsa distance formula (1.1)
nodes.statement: \dist{X}{Y} \coloneqq \ent{X' - Y'} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{X'} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Y'},
nodes.origin_citation: Green, Manners & Tao 2023 (Sumsets and entropy revisited)
nodes.label: ruz-dist-def

nodes.name: Entropic polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G = \mathbf{F}_2^n$, and suppose that $X^0_1, X^0_2$ are $G$-valued random variables. Then there is some subgroup $H \leqslant G$ such that \[ \dist{X^0_1}{U_H} + \dist{X^0_2}{U_H} \leqslant 11\dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2}, \] where $U_H$ denotes the uniform distribution on $H$. Furthermore, both $\dist{X^0_1}{U_H}$ and $\dist{X^0_2}{U_H}$ are at most $6 \dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Any two $\mathbf{F}_2^n$-valued random variables are within $11\,d[X_1^0;X_2^0]$ (total) of a uniform distribution on a subgroup.
assumptions: $G = \mathbf{F}_2^n$
$X^0_1, X^0_2$ are $G$-valued random variables
conclusions: there is some subgroup $H \leqslant G$ such that \[ \dist{X^0_1}{U_H} + \dist{X^0_2}{U_H} \leqslant 11\dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2}, \]
both $\dist{X^0_1}{U_H}$ and $\dist{X^0_2}{U_H}$ are at most $6 \dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2}$
nodes.label: pfr-entropy

nodes.name: Equivalence of entropic and combinatorial PFR
nodes.statement: The fact that \Cref{pfr-entropy} is equivalent, up to constants, to the characteristic $2$ case of Marton's original conjecture, as well as to the other combinatorial formulations of the polynomial Freiman--Ruzsa conjecture, was established in~\cite[Section 8]{gmt}.
nodes.origin_citation: Green, Manners & Tao 2023 (Sumsets and entropy revisited), Section 8
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.8 is equivalent up to constants to Marton's conjecture and its other formulations.

nodes.name: Strong PFR conjecture (approximate homomorphisms)
nodes.statement: One could consider strengthening \Cref{additive-stability} by requiring the function $h$ to take values in a $C_7$-fold sumset of the set $\{ f(x)+f(y)-f(x+y): x,y \in \mathbf{F}_2^m\}$, for some absolute constant $C_7$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 1.4 with $h$ taking values in a bounded iterated sumset of the defect set.

nodes.name: Strong PFR conjecture is false
nodes.statement: However, this ``strong PFR conjecture'' is known to be false: see~\cite{aaronson} and~\cite[Section 1.17]{tao-poincare}.

nodes.name: Polynomial Bogolyubov conjecture
nodes.statement: The \emph{polynomial Bogolyubov conjecture} (see e.g.,~\cite[Conjecture 1.5]{lovett-survey}) asserts that if $A$ is a non-empty subset of $\mathbf{F}_2^n$ of doubling at most $K$, then $2A-2A=4A$ contains a subspace of cardinality $\gg K^{-O(1)} |A|$.
nodes.statement_short: $2A-2A$ contains a subspace of size $K^{-O(1)}|A|$ when $A$ has doubling $K$.

nodes.name: Sanders' Bogolyubov-Ruzsa lemma
nodes.statement: In~\cite{sanders} it was shown that $2A-2A$ contains a subspace of size at least $\gg K^{-O(\log^3 K)} |A|$; see also a recent bilinear extension of this result in~\cite{hosseini-lovett}.
nodes.statement_short: $2A-2A$ contains a subspace of size $K^{-O(\log^3 K)}|A|$.

nodes.name: Freiman constant f(2,K)
nodes.statement: Let $f(2,K)$ denote the best constant such that every non-empty subset $A$ of $\mathbf{F}_2^n$ of doubling at most $K$ is contained in an affine subspace of cardinality at most $f(2,K) |A|$.

nodes.name: Even-Zohar's asymptotics for f(2,K)
nodes.statement: It is known that $f(2,K)$ is a piecewise linear function that can be explicitly computed for small $K$, and has the asymptotic bounds \[ \frac{2^{2K}}{4K} (1-o(1)) \leqslant f(2,K) \leqslant \frac{2^{2K}}{2K}(1+o(1))\] as $K \to \infty$; see~\cite{even-zohar} (which builds upon prior work in~\cite{diao, gt-freiman, konyagin}).
nodes.statement_short: $f(2,K)$ is piecewise linear and $\asymp 2^{2K}/K$.

nodes.name: Fixed group G and reference variables X^0_1, X^0_2
nodes.statement: Fix, for the rest of the paper, the group $G = \mathbf{F}_2^n$ and the variables $X^0_1, X^0_2$ appearing in \Cref{pfr-entropy}.

nodes.name: Constant eta = 1/9
nodes.statement: For the rest of the paper, $\eta$ will denote the constant $\frac{1}{9}$.

nodes.name: Functional tau
nodes.statement: For any two $G$-valued random variables $X_1, X_2$, we introduce the functional \begin{equation} \tau[X_1; X_2] \coloneqq \dist{X_1}{X_2} + \eta \dist{X^0_1}{X_1} + \eta \dist{X^0_2}{X_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\tau$ = Ruzsa distance plus $\eta$ times the distances to the reference variables.

nodes.name: Definition of tau (2.1)
nodes.statement: \tau[X_1; X_2] \coloneqq \dist{X_1}{X_2} + \eta \dist{X^0_1}{X_1} + \eta \dist{X^0_2}{X_2}.
nodes.label: tau-def

nodes.name: Distance-decrement proposition (tau can be decreased)
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, X_2$ be two $G$-valued random variables with $\dist{X_1}{X_2} > 0$. Then there are $G$-valued random variables $X'_1, X'_2$ such that \begin{equation} \tau[X'_1;X'_2] < \tau[X_1;X_2]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If $d[X_1;X_2]>0$ there are $X'_1,X'_2$ with strictly smaller $\tau$.
assumptions: $X_1, X_2$ be two $G$-valued random variables with $\dist{X_1}{X_2} > 0$
conclusions: there are $G$-valued random variables $X'_1, X'_2$ such that \begin{equation} \tau[X'_1;X'_2] < \tau[X_1;X_2].
nodes.label: de-prop

nodes.name: 100 percent case of entropic PFR
nodes.statement: Suppose that $X_1,X_2$ are $G$-valued random variables such that $\dist{X_1}{X_2}=0$. Then there exists a subgroup $H \leqslant G$ such that $\dist{X_1}{U_H} = \dist{X_2}{U_H} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Zero Ruzsa distance forces both variables to be at distance zero from a uniform distribution on a subgroup.
assumptions: $X_1,X_2$ are $G$-valued random variables such that $\dist{X_1}{X_2}=0$
conclusions: there exists a subgroup $H \leqslant G$ such that $\dist{X_1}{U_H} = \dist{X_2}{U_H} = 0$
nodes.label: lem:100pc

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality, $\dist{X_1}{X_1} = 0$, and so (since $G=\mathbf{F}_2^n$) we have $\dist{X_1}{-X_1} = 0$. By~\cite[Theorem~1.11(i)]{tao-entropy}, it follows that there exists a subgroup $H$ with $\dist{X_1}{U_H} = 0$. Then $\dist{X_2}{U_H}=0$ follows by the triangle inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality gives $d[X_1;-X_1]=0$; Tao's 100% inverse theorem gives $H$; triangle inequality again.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality gives d[X1;-X1]=0
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality, $\dist{X_1}{X_1} = 0$, and so (since $G=\mathbf{F}_2^n$) we have $\dist{X_1}{-X_1} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality gives d[X1;-X1]=0

nodes.name: Tao's theorem gives the subgroup H
nodes.statement: By~\cite[Theorem~1.11(i)]{tao-entropy}, it follows that there exists a subgroup $H$ with $\dist{X_1}{U_H} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Tao's theorem gives the subgroup H

nodes.name: Triangle inequality for X2
nodes.statement: Then $\dist{X_2}{U_H}=0$ follows by the triangle inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality for X2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.8 assuming Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: We choose a pair of variables $X_1,X_2$ (or more precisely, their distributions on $G$) to be any minimizer\footnote{We remark that an entropy functional minimization was previously employed by the fourth author in~\cite{tao-regularity} to give an alternative proof of the Szemer\'edi regularity lemma.} of the functional $\tau$. This optimization problem ranges over the square of the space of probability distributions on the finite set $G$. The usual topology on this space is compact, and it is straightforward that $\dist{-}{ -}$ is continuous with respect to this topology, so the minimum exists. As $(X_1,X_2)$ minimizes $\tau$, by the contrapositive of \Cref{de-prop} we must have $\dist{X_1}{X_2}=0$, and hence by \Cref{lem:100pc} there exists a subgroup $H \leqslant G$ such that $\dist{X_1}{U_H} = \dist{X_2}{U_H}=0$. Finally, we have \begin{align*} \eta (\dist{X_1^0}{U_H} + & \dist{X_2^0}{U_H})= \eta (\dist{X_1^0}{X_1} + \dist{X_2^0}{X_2}) \\ & = \tau[X_1;X_2] \leqslant \tau[X_2^0;X_1^0] = (1+2\eta) \dist{X_1^0}{X_2^0}, \end{align*} and so with our choice $\eta = \frac{1}{9}$ we obtain the first claim of \Cref{pfr-entropy}. Since $ \lvert \dist{X^0_1}{U_H} - \dist{X^0_2}{U_H} \rvert \leqslant \dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2} $ by the triangle inequality, the second statement then follows.
nodes.statement_short: Take a minimiser of $\tau$ (exists by compactness); Prop. 2.1 forces $d=0$, Lemma 2.2 gives $H$. Bound $\eta$ times the distances by $\tau(X^0_2,X^0_1)$.

nodes.name: Choose a minimiser of tau; it exists by compactness
nodes.statement: We choose a pair of variables $X_1,X_2$ (or more precisely, their distributions on $G$) to be any minimizer\footnote{We remark that an entropy functional minimization was previously employed by the fourth author in~\cite{tao-regularity} to give an alternative proof of the Szemer\'edi regularity lemma.} of the functional $\tau$. This optimization problem ranges over the square of the space of probability distributions on the finite set $G$. The usual topology on this space is compact, and it is straightforward that $\dist{-}{ -}$ is continuous with respect to this topology, so the minimum exists.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a minimiser of tau; it exists by compactness

nodes.name: Prop. 2.1 and Lemma 2.2 give H
nodes.statement: As $(X_1,X_2)$ minimizes $\tau$, by the contrapositive of \Cref{de-prop} we must have $\dist{X_1}{X_2}=0$, and hence by \Cref{lem:100pc} there exists a subgroup $H \leqslant G$ such that $\dist{X_1}{U_H} = \dist{X_2}{U_H}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Prop. 2.1 and Lemma 2.2 give H

nodes.name: Compare tau with its value at the reference pair
nodes.statement: Finally, we have \begin{align*} \eta (\dist{X_1^0}{U_H} + & \dist{X_2^0}{U_H})= \eta (\dist{X_1^0}{X_1} + \dist{X_2^0}{X_2}) \\ & = \tau[X_1;X_2] \leqslant \tau[X_2^0;X_1^0] = (1+2\eta) \dist{X_1^0}{X_2^0}, \end{align*} and so with our choice $\eta = \frac{1}{9}$ we obtain the first claim of \Cref{pfr-entropy}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare tau with its value at the reference pair

nodes.name: Second claim by the triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Since $ \lvert \dist{X^0_1}{U_H} - \dist{X^0_2}{U_H} \rvert \leqslant \dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2} $ by the triangle inequality, the second statement then follows.
nodes.statement_short: Second claim by the triangle inequality

nodes.name: Algorithmic variant of the proof
nodes.statement: The proof of \Cref{de-prop} is completely algorithmic, but our use of compactness here means that the proof of \Cref{pfr-entropy} is not. However, our argument can be modified to give a completely algorithmic proof, at the expense of slightly worse constants. One approach is to prove \Cref{de-prop} with~\eqref{d-opt} replaced by the stronger bound \begin{equation} \dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \leqslant (1 - \eta') \dist{X_1}{X_2} - \eta' \dist{X'_1}{X_1} - \eta' \dist{X'_2}{X_2}, \end{equation} for some value $\eta'$ rather smaller than $\eta=\frac{1}{9}$. The proof is very similar and follows the same strategy as that outlined in \Cref{sec3}. This variant is perhaps even slightly easier to follow than the current proof, since the `fixed' variables $X_1^0, X_2^0$ no longer play a role. Once~\eqref{proper-decrement} is established, it can be applied iteratively to give a sequence $(X_1^{t}, X_2^{t})$, $t = 0,1,\dots$ for which $\dist{X_1^{t}}{X_2^{t}}$ decays exponentially. In particular, for some $T = O(\log \dist{X^0_1}{X^0_2})$ we have $\dist{X_1^{T}}{X_2^{T}} \leqslant \varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0$ is the absolute constant appearing in~\cite[Proposition 1.3]{gmt}. By that result, $X_1^{T}$ and $X_2^{T}$ are both close to some variable $U_H$. One can then control the distance of $U_H$ from the original variables $X^0_1, X^0_2$ by summing~\eqref{proper-decrement} over $0 \leqslant t < T$ and applying the Ruzsa triangle inequality repeatedly. A version of this argument will be given in detail in our subsequent paper~\cite{ggmt-pfr-odd}.
nodes.statement_short: Proving a stronger multiplicative decrement gives an iterative, compactness-free proof with worse constants.
nodes.label: quant

nodes.name: Proper decrement (2.3)
nodes.statement: \dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \leqslant (1 - \eta') \dist{X_1}{X_2} - \eta' \dist{X'_1}{X_1} - \eta' \dist{X'_2}{X_2},
nodes.label: proper-decrement

nodes.name: Weak Bogolyubov-type consequence
nodes.statement: We sketch one further consequence of the variant argument discussed in \Cref{quant} above, namely a weak Bogulyubov-type result: if $|A+A| \leqslant K|A|$, then there is a subspace $H$ of $G$ of cardinality $\gg K^{-O(1)} |A|$ that is contained in an iterated sumset $mA$ for some $m = O(\log^{O(1)}(2+K))$. Indeed, if takes $X^0_1 = X^0_2 = U_A$ as in \Cref{equiv-app} and runs the above iteration, we see inductively from an inspection of the construction that each pair $X_1^t, X_2^t$ of random variables produced by the iterative process is contained in $m_t A$ for some $m_t = O(1)^t$. Since it only takes $O(\log\log K)$ steps for the doubling constant to get within range of $\varepsilon_0$, one can check (by inspection of the argument in~\cite[Proposition 1.3]{gmt}) that the group $H$ produced is then contained in $mA$ for some $m = O(\log^{O(1)}(2+K))$, and the claim then follows after some routine verifications.
nodes.statement_short: The iteration yields a subspace of size $K^{-O(1)}|A|$ inside $mA$ with $m=O(\log^{O(1)}K)$.
nodes.label: bog-remark

nodes.name: Distance k
nodes.statement: Let $k$ denote the quantity $k \coloneqq \dist{X_1}{X_2}$.

nodes.name: Notation O(eta k)
nodes.statement: For the following preliminary discussion we write various estimates as $O(\eta k)$ for simplicity.

nodes.name: Independent copies tilde X_1, tilde X_2
nodes.statement: To describe the choices we will try, consider a four-tuple of independent random variables $X_1, X_2, \tilde X_1, \tilde X_2$ where $X_1,\tilde X_1$ are copies of $X_1$ and $X_2,\tilde X_2$ are copies of $X_2$; we can in fact assume that all six variables $X_1,X_2,\tilde X_1,\tilde X_2,X^0_1,X^0_2$ are independent.

nodes.name: Candidate pairs: sums and fibres
nodes.statement: Our primary choices for $(X'_1, X'_2)$ will be sums \begin{equation} X'_1 = X_1 + \tilde X_2,\qquad X'_2 = X_2 + \tilde X_1 \end{equation} or \begin{equation} X'_1 = X_1 + \tilde X_1,\qquad X'_2 = X_2 + \tilde X_2 \end{equation} or alternatively `fibres' \begin{equation} X'_1 = (X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_2= g),\qquad X'_2 = (X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_1 = g') \end{equation} or \begin{equation} X'_1 = (X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_1= g),\qquad X'_2 = (X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_2 = g') \end{equation} for $g, g' \in G$.
nodes.statement_short: The candidates $X'_i$: sums $X_i+\tilde X_j$ (3.1)-(3.2) or fibres $(X_i|X_i+\tilde X_j=g)$ (3.3)-(3.4).

nodes.name: Sum choice (3.1)
nodes.statement: X'_1 = X_1 + \tilde X_2,\qquad X'_2 = X_2 + \tilde X_1
nodes.label: sum-1

nodes.name: Sum choice (3.2)
nodes.statement: X'_1 = X_1 + \tilde X_1,\qquad X'_2 = X_2 + \tilde X_2
nodes.label: sum-2

nodes.name: Fibre choice (3.3)
nodes.statement: X'_1 = (X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_2= g),\qquad X'_2 = (X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_1 = g')
nodes.label: fiber-1

nodes.name: Fibre choice (3.4)
nodes.statement: X'_1 = (X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_1= g),\qquad X'_2 = (X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_2 = g')
nodes.label: fiber-2

nodes.name: Heuristic first estimate (I_1 small)
nodes.statement: What we find in this case is that if neither choice~\eqref{sum-1},~\eqref{fiber-1} works to prove~\eqref{d-opt} then we have an upper bound \begin{equation} I_1 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } = O(\eta k). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If sums (3.1) and fibres (3.3) fail, $I_1=O(\eta k)$.

nodes.name: I_1 = O(eta k) (3.5)
nodes.statement: I_1 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } = O(\eta k).
nodes.label: first-est-a

nodes.name: Heuristic second estimate (I_2 small)
nodes.statement: Similarly, if neither choice~\eqref{sum-2},~\eqref{fiber-2} works to prove~\eqref{d-opt}, we obtain a bound \begin{equation} I_2 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } = O(\eta k). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If (3.2) and (3.4) fail, $I_2=O(\eta k)$.

nodes.name: I_2 = O(eta k) (3.6)
nodes.statement: I_2 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } = O(\eta k).
nodes.label: second-est-a

nodes.name: Heuristic third estimate (I_3 = I_2)
nodes.statement: Finally, \begin{equation} I_3 \coloneqq \bigI{ \tilde X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } = O(\eta k), \end{equation} since in fact we have $I_2 = I_3$, as may be seen by interchanging the names of $\tilde X_1$ and $X_1$.
nodes.statement_short: $I_3=O(\eta k)$ too, since $I_3=I_2$ by symmetry.

nodes.name: I_3 = O(eta k) (3.7)
nodes.statement: I_3 \coloneqq \bigI{ \tilde X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } = O(\eta k),
nodes.label: third-est-a

nodes.name: Exact case: T_1, T_2, T_3 pairwise independent
nodes.statement: Suppose first for simplicity that the mutual informations in~\eqref{first-est-a},\ \eqref{second-est-a} and~\eqref{third-est-a} were zero rather than merely small. It follows that for any $s$ in the support of $X_1+X_2+ \tilde X_1+\tilde X_2$, the three random variables \begin{align} \nonumber T_1&= (X_1+X_2 |X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2=s),\\ \nonumber T_2&=(X_1+\tilde X_1 |X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2=s), \\ T_3&=(\tilde X_1+X_2 |X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2=s) \end{align} are pairwise independent.
nodes.statement_short: If $I_1=I_2=I_3=0$, the conditioned sums $T_1,T_2,T_3$ are pairwise independent.

nodes.name: Variables T_1, T_2, T_3 (3.8)
nodes.statement: \nonumber T_1&= (X_1+X_2 |X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2=s),\\ \nonumber T_2&=(X_1+\tilde X_1 |X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2=s), \\ T_3&=(\tilde X_1+X_2 |X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2=s)
nodes.label: three-variables

nodes.name: T_1 + T_2 + T_3 = 0
nodes.statement: We also note that $T_1+T_2+T_3$ is constant (in fact it is identically zero).

nodes.name: Pairwise independent trio with constant sum has zero distances
nodes.statement: However, for any trio $(T_1,T_2,T_3)$ of pairwise independent random variables such that $T_1+T_2+T_3$ is constant, a short calculation shows that \[\dist{T_1}{T_2} = \ent{T_3} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{T_1} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{T_2} \] and similarly for cyclic permutations, hence \begin{equation} \dist{T_1}{T_2} + \dist{T_1}{T_3} + \dist{T_2}{T_3} = 0 \end{equation} and so, taking $X'_1$ and $X'_2$ to be some pair of $T_1,T_2,T_3$, we have $\dist{X_1'}{X_2'} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: For pairwise independent $T_i$ with constant sum, the three pairwise Ruzsa distances sum to 0.

nodes.name: Sum of the three distances vanishes (3.9)
nodes.label: eq:i-eq-0

nodes.name: Role of entropic Balog-Szemeredi-Gowers in the plan
nodes.statement: If the three variables in~\eqref{three-variables} are merely `almost pairwise independent', as in~\eqref{first-est-a} and~\eqref{second-est-a}, then things are less straightforward. Very roughly, sums of non-independent random variables are to sums of independent random variables as \emph{partial} sumsets $A+_E B$ along a bipartite graph $E$ are to full sumsets $A+B$. Hence, it is natural to apply a variant of the entropic Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers lemma due to the fourth author~\cite[Lemma 3.3]{tao-entropy} (reproduced as \Cref{lem-bsg} here) to pass from the `almost independent' variables $(T_1,T_2)$ as above, for which $\ent{T_1+T_2}-\tfrac12 \ent{T_1} - \tfrac12 \ent{T_2}$ is small (or even negative), to variables $X_1',X_2'$ with $\dist{X_1'}{X_2'} = O(\eta k)$. These variables $X'_1,X'_2$, which are given to us by \Cref{lem-bsg}, now establish~\eqref{d-opt}. Examining the proof of \Cref{lem-bsg} carefully, the final choice of $X'_1$ that comes out of this argument is of the form \begin{equation} (X_1 + X_2 \,|\, \tilde X_1+ X_2 = t, X_1 + \tilde X_2 = s+t) \end{equation} or a related quantity obtained by permuting the variables, and similarly for $X'_2$ (using the same $s,t$ for both $X_1'$ and $X_2'$).
nodes.statement_short: In the almost-independent case entropic BSG produces $X'_1,X'_2$ of the form (3.10) with $d=O(\eta k)$.

nodes.name: Form of the BSG output (3.10)
nodes.statement: (X_1 + X_2 \,|\, \tilde X_1+ X_2 = t, X_1 + \tilde X_2 = s+t)
nodes.label: from-bsg

nodes.name: K = e^k
nodes.statement: In this discussion is convenient to write $K \coloneqq e^k$.

nodes.name: Random subset of a subgroup
nodes.statement: Consider first the case in which $A_1=A_2=A$ and $A$ is a random subset of some subgroup $H \leqslant \mathbf{F}_2^n$ with density $K^{-1}$ in $H$. Then (almost surely) $\dist{X_1}{X_2} \approx k$. In this case the choice~\eqref{sum-2}, that is to say $X'_1 = X_1 + \tilde X_1$ and $X'_2 = X_2 + \tilde X_2$, immediately establishes~\eqref{d-opt}. Indeed both $X'_1$ and $X'_2$ are close to the uniform distribution $U_H$ on $H$, so $\dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \approx 0$ and $\dist{X'_i}{X_i}\approx k/2$ for $i=1,2$, and~\eqref{d-opt} follows, with room to spare, by the triangle inequality.
nodes.statement_short: For a random dense subset of a subgroup the sums (3.2) already decrease $\tau$.

nodes.name: Union of independent cosets
nodes.statement: Consider next the case in which $A_1 = \bigcup_{i = 1}^{m} (x_i + H)$ and $A_2 = \bigcup_{i=1}^m (y_i+ H)$, where $H < \mathbf{F}_2^n$ is a subgroup and the $x_i+H$ and $y_i+H$ are linearly independent in $G/H$. Setting $m \coloneqq K$ gives $\dist{X_1}{X_2} \approx k$. In this case one can obtain~\eqref{d-opt} with the choice~\eqref{fiber-1}, that is to say $X'_1 = (X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_2 = g)$ and $X'_2 = (X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_1 = g')$ for any $g,g' \in A_1+A_2$. Indeed, $X'_1$ is the uniform distribution on $A_1 \cap (A_2 + g)$, which if $g \in x_i+y_j+H$ is exactly the coset $x_i+H$ of $H$ (by linear independence). Similarly, $X'_2$ is uniform on a coset $y_j'+H$, so $\dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \approx 0$ and again~\eqref{d-opt} follows. (Using the fibres in~\eqref{fiber-2} also gives a contradiction in this case, but the analysis is slightly more involved, since $A_1 \cap (A_1 + g)$ is typically a union of two cosets of $H$.)
nodes.statement_short: For unions of $K$ independent cosets the fibres (3.3) decrease $\tau$.

nodes.name: Random subsets of unions of cosets (endgame needed)
nodes.statement: Here is a third example, a sort of combination of the previous two, for which the choices~\eqref{sum-1},~\eqref{sum-2},~\eqref{fiber-1} and~\eqref{fiber-2} all fail to work. Let $A_1',A_2'$ be (independent) random subsets of density $1/m$ of the sets $A_1,A_2$ from the previous example, where now $m = \sqrt{K}$. One may then check that $X_1 + \tilde X_1, X_2 + \tilde X_2$ resemble the uniform distribution on the union of $\approx K/2$ cosets of $H$, so $\dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \approx k - O(1)$ and we do not obtain~\eqref{d-opt} (if $k$ is large) with the choice~\eqref{sum-2}. The case of~\eqref{sum-1} is similar. On the other hand, the variables $(X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_2 = g)$, $(X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_1 = g')$ will be uniform on $A_1 \cap (A_2 + g)$ and $A_2 \cap (A_1+g')$ respectively, and such sets will typically (when non-empty) resemble random subsets of a coset of $H$, of density $1/m^2 \approx 1/K$. For these variables we also have $\dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \approx k$, and so we do not obtain~\eqref{d-opt} with the choice~\eqref{fiber-1}. The case of~\eqref{fiber-2} is broadly similar. We therefore proceed to the endgame and consider the three variables in~\eqref{three-variables}. Since $X_1+X_2$ is roughly uniform on $B \coloneqq \bigcup_{i,j} (x_i+y_j+H)$, a similar analysis to the second example shows that $(X_1+X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1 + \tilde X_2 = s)$ is roughly uniform on $B \cap (B+s)$, which is typically a union of four cosets of $H$, and similarly for $(\tilde X_1+X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1 + \tilde X_2 = s)$. Moreover, one can check that these two variables are `50\% independent' (in that knowing one of them narrows the choice of the other to two cosets of $H$). If we then apply \Cref{lem-bsg}, we find variables $X'_1$, $X'_2$ of the form given in~\eqref{from-bsg}. In other words, $X'_1$ is a sum of two variables of the form $(X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_2 = a)$ and $(X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_1 = b)$. Each will be uniform on a random subset of a coset of $H$, and adding them together will give something close to uniform on a coset of $H$. The case of $X'_2$ is similar, so we get $\dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \approx 0$ and~\eqref{d-opt} follows. (Again, permuting the variables may give slighly different conclusions.)
nodes.statement_short: All four sum/fibre choices fail; the endgame with entropic BSG succeeds.

nodes.name: Discrete Gaussians over Z
nodes.statement: Finally, we consider a further example over $G = \mathbf{Z}$ instead of $\mathbf{F}_2^n$. Take $X_1,X_2$ to have a `discrete Gaussian' distribution $p(x) = C_0 e^{-x^2/2r^2}$ with some large `width' $r$ and a normalizing constant $C_0$. By~\cite[Theorem~1.13]{tao-entropy}, the distance $\dist{X_1}{X_2} \approx \frac12 \log 2$ is roughly minimal among random variables on $\mathbf{Z}$ with large entropy, and hence \Cref{de-prop} cannot hold over $\mathbf{Z}$ in the form stated. Concretely, one can show that sums $X_i+\tilde X_j$ as in~\eqref{sum-1},~\eqref{sum-2} are (roughly) discrete Gaussians of width $\sqrt2r$, and fibres $(X_i | X_i+\tilde X_j)$ as in~\eqref{fiber-1},~\eqref{fiber-2} are (shifted) discrete Gaussians of width about $r/\sqrt2$. Hence, all these have essentially the same value of $\dist{-}{-}$, and there is no way of `improving' these variables with any of the choices considered in \Cref{first,second}. One could also see directly that the conditional near-independence statements such as \[ \I{X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1 + \tilde X_2} \approx 0 \] do indeed hold for discrete Gaussians. In the above one-dimensional example, the entropic doubling constant is bounded, and so this example does not, by itself, present a strong obstruction to the entire approach. However, by considering discrete gaussian examples in a high-dimensional lattice $\mathbf{Z}^d$, the entropic doubling constant is now close to $\frac{d}{2} \log 2$, which is unbounded, and all the moves considered previously do not significantly reduce this constant. Even though discrete Gaussians over $\mathbf{F}_2$ do not exist, this example places significant constraints on what we can hope to prove in general. In particular, it shows that the endgame argument must `see' the finite characteristic in an essential way.
nodes.statement_short: Discrete Gaussians show Prop. 2.1 fails over $\mathbf{Z}$, so the endgame must use characteristic 2.

nodes.name: Contrapositive hypothesis: (X_1, X_2) minimises tau
nodes.statement: Thus, suppose henceforth that we have a pair $(X_1, X_2)$ of $G$-valued random variables with $\dist{X_1}{X_2} = k$ for some $k$, and suppose that \begin{equation} \tau[X'_1;X'_2] \geqslant \tau[X_1;X_2] \end{equation} for every pair of $G$-valued random variables $(X'_1, X'_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $d[X_1;X_2]=k$ and no pair $(X'_1,X'_2)$ has smaller $\tau$.

nodes.name: tau not decreased (3.11)
nodes.statement: \tau[X'_1;X'_2] \geqslant \tau[X_1;X_2]
nodes.label: to-contradict'

nodes.name: Hypothesis in terms of distances
nodes.statement: Using the definition of $\tau$ (see~\eqref{tau-def}) we may rewrite~\eqref{to-contradict'} as \begin{equation} \dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \geqslant k - \costa{X'_1} - \costb{X'_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The hypothesis says $d[X'_1;X'_2]\ge k$ minus the $\eta$-penalties.

nodes.name: Hypothesis rewritten (3.12)
nodes.statement: \dist{X'_1}{X'_2} \geqslant k - \costa{X'_1} - \costb{X'_2}.
nodes.label: to-contradict

nodes.name: First estimate (I_1 <= 2 eta k)
nodes.statement: I_1 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } \leqslant 2 \eta k
nodes.statement_short: $I_1=I[X_1+X_2:\tilde X_1+X_2\mid X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2]\le 2\eta k$.
conclusions: I_1 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } \leqslant 2 \eta k
nodes.label: first-est

nodes.name: Second estimate (bound on I_2)
nodes.statement: I_2 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } \leqslant 2 \eta k + \frac{2 \eta (2 \eta k - I_1)}{1 - \eta}
nodes.statement_short: $I_2\le 2\eta k+2\eta(2\eta k-I_1)/(1-\eta)$.
conclusions: I_2 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : X_1 + \tilde X_1 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } \leqslant 2 \eta k + \frac{2 \eta (2 \eta k - I_1)}{1 - \eta}
nodes.label: second-est

nodes.name: Conditioned hypothesis
nodes.statement: Note that~\eqref{to-contradict} implies a conditioned version of itself: for any random variables $(X_1',Y_1)$ and $(X_2',Y_2)$ we may apply~\eqref{to-contradict} with $X'_1, X'_2$ replaced by each of the conditioned random variables $(X'_1 | Y_1 = y_1) , (X'_2 | Y_2 = y_2)$, obtaining \begin{align*} & \dist{(X'_1 | Y_1 = y_1)}{(X'_2 | Y_2 = y_2)} \\ & \qquad\qquad\qquad \geqslant k \begin{aligned}[t] &- \costa{(X'_1 | Y_1 = y_1)} \\ &- \costb{(X'_2 | Y_2 = y_2)}. \end{aligned} \end{align*} Multiplying by $p_{Y_1}(y_1) p_{Y_2}(y_2)$ and summing, we have \begin{align} \nonumber \dist{X'_1 | Y_1}{X'_2 | Y_2} \geqslant k &- \costa{X'_1 | Y_1} \\ &- \costb{X'_2 | Y_2}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Averaging (3.12) over conditionings gives the same lower bound for conditional distances.

nodes.name: Conditioned hypothesis (3.15)
nodes.statement: \nonumber \dist{X'_1 | Y_1}{X'_2 | Y_2} \geqslant k &- \costa{X'_1 | Y_1} \\ &- \costb{X'_2 | Y_2}.
nodes.label: to-contradict-avg

nodes.name: Odd characteristic
nodes.statement: We will handle the case $p$ odd in our forthcoming paper~\cite{ggmt-pfr-odd}. All of the above steps go through, except for the final contradiction in the `endgame' where we used an argument specific to characteristic $2$. To get a contradiction in characteristic $p$, it is necessary to run a variant of the argument with a $p$-partite `distance' function $\operatorname{D}[X_1;\dots; X_p]$ replacing $\dist{X_1}{X_2}$ as the main term in the functional to be minimized. This introduces additional notational complexity: for instance we now have an array $(X_{ij})_{i,j \in \mathbf{F}_p}$ of random variables, and the fibring lemma must be generalized to this $p$-partite distance and applied $p-1$ times.
nodes.statement_short: All steps but the endgame carry over to odd $p$; there one minimises a $p$-partite distance.

nodes.name: Fibring lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\pi \colon H \to H'$ be a homomorphism between abelian groups and let $Z_1,Z_2$ be $H$-valued random variables. Then we have \[ \dist{Z_1}{Z_2} \geqslant \dist{\pi(Z_1)}{\pi(Z_2)} + \dist{Z_1|\pi(Z_1)}{Z_2 |\pi(Z_2)} \] where the notation is as in~\eqref{cond-dist-def}. Moreover, if $Z_1,Z_2$ are taken to be independent, then the difference between the two sides is \begin{equation} \bigI{ Z_1 - Z_2 : (\pi(Z_1), \pi(Z_2)) \; | \; \pi(Z_1 - Z_2)}. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: Green, Manners & Tao 2023 (Sumsets and entropy revisited), Proposition 1.4
nodes.statement_short: Ruzsa distance splits into the distance of the images under a homomorphism plus the conditional distance of the fibres, up to a conditional mutual information.
assumptions: $\pi \colon H \to H'$ be a homomorphism between abelian groups and let $Z_1,Z_2$ be $H$-valued random variables
conclusions: \dist{Z_1}{Z_2} \geqslant \dist{\pi(Z_1)}{\pi(Z_2)} + \dist{Z_1|\pi(Z_1)}{Z_2 |\pi(Z_2)}
nodes.label: projections-1

nodes.name: Proof of the fibring lemma
nodes.statement: Let $Z_1,Z_2$ be independent throughout. We have \begin{align*} & \bigdist{Z_1 |\pi(Z_1)}{ Z_2 |\pi(Z_2)} \\ & = \bigH{ Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_2)} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Z_1 | \pi(Z_1)} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Z_2 | \pi(Z_2)} \\ & \leqslant \bigH{ Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1-Z_2)} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Z_1 | \pi(Z_1)} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Z_2 | \pi(Z_2)} \\ & = \dist{Z_1}{Z_2} - \dist{\pi(Z_1)}{\pi(Z_2)}. \end{align*} In the middle step, we used submodularity of entropy, and in the last step we used the fact that \[ \bigH{ Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1-Z_2)} = \ent{Z_1 - Z_2} - \ent{\pi(Z_1-Z_2)}\] (since $Z_1 - Z_2$ determines $\pi(Z_1 - Z_2)$) and that \[ \ent{Z_i| \pi(Z_i)} = \ent{Z_i} - \ent{\pi(Z_i)}\] (since $Z_i$ determines $\pi(Z_i)$). This gives the claimed inequality. The difference between the two sides is precisely \[ \bigH{Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1 - Z_2)} - \bigH{Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_2)}.\] To rewrite this in terms of (conditional) mutual information, we use the identity \[ \ent{A|B} - \ent{A | B,C} = \I{A : C | B},\] taking $A \coloneqq Z_1 - Z_2$, $B \coloneqq \pi(Z_1 - Z_2)$ and $C \coloneqq (\pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_{2}))$, and noting that in this case $\ent{A | B,C} = \ent{A | C}$ since $C$ uniquely determines $B$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand both sides in entropies; submodularity gives the inequality and the defect is a conditional mutual information.

nodes.name: Expand the conditional distance and apply submodularity
nodes.statement: Let $Z_1,Z_2$ be independent throughout. We have \begin{align*} & \bigdist{Z_1 |\pi(Z_1)}{ Z_2 |\pi(Z_2)} \\ & = \bigH{ Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_2)} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Z_1 | \pi(Z_1)} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Z_2 | \pi(Z_2)} \\ & \leqslant \bigH{ Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1-Z_2)} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Z_1 | \pi(Z_1)} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Z_2 | \pi(Z_2)} \\ & = \dist{Z_1}{Z_2} - \dist{\pi(Z_1)}{\pi(Z_2)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the conditional distance and apply submodularity

nodes.statement: In the middle step, we used submodularity of entropy, and in the last step we used the fact that \[ \bigH{ Z_1 - Z_2 | \pi(Z_1-Z_2)} = \ent{Z_1 - Z_2} - \ent{\pi(Z_1-Z_2)}\] (since $Z_1 - Z_2$ determines $\pi(Z_1 - Z_2)$) and that \[ \ent{Z_i| \pi(Z_i)} = \ent{Z_i} - \ent{\pi(Z_i)}\] (since $Z_i$ determines $\pi(Z_i)$). This gives the claimed inequality.

nodes.name: Identify the defect as I[A:C|B]
nodes.statement: To rewrite this in terms of (conditional) mutual information, we use the identity \[ \ent{A|B} - \ent{A | B,C} = \I{A : C | B},\] taking $A \coloneqq Z_1 - Z_2$, $B \coloneqq \pi(Z_1 - Z_2)$ and $C \coloneqq (\pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_{2}))$, and noting that in this case $\ent{A | B,C} = \ent{A | C}$ since $C$ uniquely determines $B$. This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Fibring identity for four independent variables
nodes.statement: Let $Y_1,Y_2,Y_3$ and $Y_4$ be independent random variables taking values in some abelian group $G$. Then \begin{align*} \nonumber & \dist{Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2-Y_4} + \bigdist{Y_1|Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2|Y_2-Y_4} \\ &\qquad + \bigI{ Y_1-Y_2 : Y_2 - Y_4 | Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4 } = \dist{Y_1}{Y_2} + \dist{Y_3}{Y_4}. \end{align*}
assumptions: $Y_1,Y_2,Y_3$ and $Y_4$ be independent random variables taking values in some abelian group $G$
conclusions: \begin{align*} \nonumber & \dist{Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2-Y_4} + \bigdist{Y_1|Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2|Y_2-Y_4} \\ &\qquad + \bigI{ Y_1-Y_2 : Y_2 - Y_4 | Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4 } = \dist{Y_1}{Y_2} + \dist{Y_3}{Y_4}. \end{align*}
nodes.label: cor-fibre

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.2
nodes.statement: We apply \Cref{projections-1} with $H \coloneqq G \times G$, $H' \coloneqq G$, $\pi$ the subtraction homomorphism $\pi(x,y) \coloneqq x-y$, and with the random variables $Z_1 \coloneqq (Y_1,Y_3)$ and $Z_2 \coloneqq (Y_2,Y_4)$. Then by independence we easily calculate \[ \dist{Z_1}{Z_2} = \dist{Y_1}{Y_2} + \dist{Y_3}{Y_4} \] while by definition \[ \dist{\pi(Z_1)}{\pi(Z_2)} = \dist{Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2-Y_4}. \] Furthermore, \[ \dist{Z_1|\pi(Z_1)}{Z_2|\pi(Z_2)} = \dist{Y_1|Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2|Y_2-Y_4}, \] since $Z_1=(Y_1,Y_3)$ and $Y_1$ are linked by an invertible affine transformation once $\pi(Z_1)=Y_1-Y_3$ is fixed, and similarly for $Z_2$ and $Y_2$. Finally, we have \begin{align*} &\bigI{Z_1 - Z_2 : (\pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_2)) \,|\, \pi(Z_1) + \pi(Z_2)} \\ &\ = \bigI{(Y_1-Y_2, Y_3-Y_4) : (Y_1-Y_3, Y_2-Y_4) \,|\, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4} \\ &\ = \bigI{Y_1-Y_2 : Y_2-Y_4 \,|\, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4} \end{align*} where in the last line we used the fact that $(Y_1-Y_2, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4)$ uniquely determine $Y_3-Y_4$ and similarly $(Y_2-Y_4, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4)$ uniquely determine $Y_1-Y_3$.

nodes.name: Apply the fibring lemma to subtraction on G x G
nodes.statement: We apply \Cref{projections-1} with $H \coloneqq G \times G$, $H' \coloneqq G$, $\pi$ the subtraction homomorphism $\pi(x,y) \coloneqq x-y$, and with the random variables $Z_1 \coloneqq (Y_1,Y_3)$ and $Z_2 \coloneqq (Y_2,Y_4)$.

nodes.name: Compute the unconditioned distances
nodes.statement: Then by independence we easily calculate \[ \dist{Z_1}{Z_2} = \dist{Y_1}{Y_2} + \dist{Y_3}{Y_4} \] while by definition \[ \dist{\pi(Z_1)}{\pi(Z_2)} = \dist{Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2-Y_4}. \]

nodes.name: Identify the conditional distances
nodes.statement: Furthermore, \[ \dist{Z_1|\pi(Z_1)}{Z_2|\pi(Z_2)} = \dist{Y_1|Y_1-Y_3}{Y_2|Y_2-Y_4}, \] since $Z_1=(Y_1,Y_3)$ and $Y_1$ are linked by an invertible affine transformation once $\pi(Z_1)=Y_1-Y_3$ is fixed, and similarly for $Z_2$ and $Y_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the conditional distances

nodes.name: Identify the mutual information term
nodes.statement: Finally, we have \begin{align*} &\bigI{Z_1 - Z_2 : (\pi(Z_1),\pi(Z_2)) \,|\, \pi(Z_1) + \pi(Z_2)} \\ &\ = \bigI{(Y_1-Y_2, Y_3-Y_4) : (Y_1-Y_3, Y_2-Y_4) \,|\, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4} \\ &\ = \bigI{Y_1-Y_2 : Y_2-Y_4 \,|\, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4} \end{align*} where in the last line we used the fact that $(Y_1-Y_2, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4)$ uniquely determine $Y_3-Y_4$ and similarly $(Y_2-Y_4, Y_1-Y_2-Y_3+Y_4)$ uniquely determine $Y_1-Y_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the mutual information term

nodes.statement: Of course, in our main characteristic $2$ setting, the minus signs in \Cref{projections-1,cor-fibre} may be replaced with plus signs.

nodes.statement_short: Test the hypothesis on the sum pair (3.1) and the fibre pair (3.3) via the fibring identity. Lemma 5.2 bounds the $\eta$-penalties by $2k$.

nodes.name: Recall the standing hypotheses
nodes.statement: Recall that in this and subsequent sections we are working on the assumption that~\eqref{to-contradict} and its conditioned variant~\eqref{to-contradict-avg} hold, aiming to prove that $k = 0$ and hence conclude (the contrapositive of) Proposition~\ref{de-prop}. Recall also that $X_1, X_2, \tilde X_1, \tilde X_2$ are independent random variables, with $X_1,\tilde X_1$ copies of $X_1$ and $X_2,\tilde X_2$ copies of $X_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the standing hypotheses

nodes.name: State the goal (3.13)
nodes.statement: In this section we establish the upper bound~\eqref{first-est}, which was that \[ I_1 \coloneqq \bigI{ X_1+X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 | X_1+X_2+\tilde X_1+\tilde X_2 } \leqslant 2 \eta k. \]

nodes.statement: We apply \Cref{cor-fibre} (and Remark \ref{rem:char2}) with the choice \[ (Y_1,Y_2,Y_3,Y_4) \coloneqq (X_1, X_2, \tilde X_2, \tilde X_1). \] It gives \begin{align} \nonumber &\dist{X_1+\tilde X_2}{X_2+\tilde X_1} + \bigdist{X_1|X_1+\tilde X_2}{X_2|X_2+\tilde X_1} \\ &\quad + \bigI{ X_1+ X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 \,|\, X_1 + X_2 + \tilde X_1 + \tilde X_2 } = 2k, \end{align} since $\dist{X_1}{X_2} = k$.

nodes.statement: \nonumber &\dist{X_1+\tilde X_2}{X_2+\tilde X_1} + \bigdist{X_1|X_1+\tilde X_2}{X_2|X_2+\tilde X_1} \\ &\quad + \bigI{ X_1+ X_2 : \tilde X_1 + X_2 \,|\, X_1 + X_2 + \tilde X_1 + \tilde X_2 } = 2k,

nodes.statement: Applying~\eqref{to-contradict},~\eqref{to-contradict-avg}, we have \begin{align*} \dist{X_1+\tilde X_2}{X_2+\tilde X_1} \geqslant k &- \costa{X_1+\tilde X_2} \\& \qquad- \costb{X_2+\tilde X_1} \end{align*} and \begin{align} \nonumber & \dist{X_1|X_1+\tilde X_2}{X_2|X_2+\tilde X_1} \\ \nonumber & \qquad\quad \geqslant k - \costa{X_1 | X_1 + \tilde X_2} \\ & \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad - \costb{X_2 | X_2 + \tilde X_1}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 and the Kaimanovich-Vershik-Madiman inequality
nodes.statement: We pause to state some lemmas which we will use for bounding a number of similar expressions, both here and in the next two sections. The first is a bound relating conditioned and unconditioned variants of the Ruzsa distance. \begin{lemma} Suppose that $(X, Z)$ and $(Y, W)$ are random variables, where $X, Y$ take values in some abelian group. Then \[ \dist{X | Z}{Y | W} \leqslant \dist{X}{Y} + \tfrac{1}{2} \I{X : Z} + \tfrac{1}{2} \I{Y : W}.\] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} The definition of conditional distance is given in~\eqref{cond-dist-def}. Using the alternative expression~\eqref{cond-dist-alt}, if $(X',Z'), (Y',W')$ are independent copies of the variables $(X,Z)$, $(Y,W)$, we have \begin{align*} \dist{X | Z}{Y | W} &= \ent{X'-Y'|Z',W'} - \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{X'|Z'} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Y'|W'} \\ &\leqslant \ent{X'-Y'}- \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{X'|Z'} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Y'|W'} \\ &= \dist{X'}{Y'} + \tfrac{1}{2} \I{X' : Z'} + \tfrac{1}{2} \I{Y' : W'}. \end{align*} Here, in the middle step we used~\eqref{cond-dec}, and in the last step we used the definitions of $\dist{-}{-}$ and $\I{-}$. \end{proof} In the proof of the next lemma we will use the fact that, for any independent random variables $X, Y, Z$ taking values in an abelian group, we have the inequality \begin{equation} \ent{X + Y + Z} - \ent{X + Y} \leqslant \ent{Y+Z} - \ent{Y}. \end{equation} This is a result of Madiman~\cite[Theorem I]{madiman}, and is a more general form of an inequality of Kaimanovich and Vershik~\cite[Proposition 1.3]{kv}. It can be viewed as an entropy analogue of an inequality of Pl\"unnecke~\cite{plunnecke}. For the convenience of the reader, we give the proof in \Cref{entropy-app}. \begin{lemma} Let $X, Y, Z$ be random variables taking values in some abelian group, and with $Y, Z$ independent. Then we have\footnote{We thank Floris van Doorn for noting a sign discrepancy in a previous version of this statement, which was uncovered as part of the effort to formalize the results of this paper in {\tt Lean 4}.} \begin{align}\nonumber \dist{X}{Y - Z} - \dist{X}{Y} & \leqslant \tfrac{1}{2} (\ent{Y-Z} - \ent{Y}) \\ & = \tfrac{1}{2} \dist{Y}{Z} + \tfrac{1}{4} \ent{Z} - \tfrac{1}{4} \ent{Y} \end{align} and \begin{align}\nonumber \dist{X}{Y|Y-Z} - \dist{X}{Y} & \leqslant \tfrac{1}{2} \bigl(\ent{Y-Z} - \ent{Z}\bigr) \\ & = \tfrac{1}{2} \dist{Y}{Z} + \tfrac{1}{4} \ent{Y} - \tfrac{1}{4} \ent{Z}. \end{align} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} We first prove~\eqref{lem51-a}. We may assume (taking an independent copy) that $X$ is independent of $Y, Z$. Then we have \begin{align*} \dist{X}{Y-Z} & - \dist{X}{Y} \\ & = \ent{X - Y + Z} - \ent{X-Y} - \tfrac{1}{2}\ent{Y - Z} + \tfrac{1}{2} \ent{Y}.\end{align*} Combining this with~\eqref{kv-2} (applied with $Y$ replaced by $-Y$) gives the required bound. The second form of the result is immediate from the definition of $\dist{Y}{Z}$, since $Y, Z$ are independent. Turning to~\eqref{ruzsa-3}, we have \begin{align*} \I{Y : Y-Z} & = \ent{Y} + \ent{Y - Z} - \ent{Y, Y - Z} \\ & = \ent{Y} + \ent{Y - Z} - \ent{Y, Z} = \ent{Y - Z} - \ent{Z},\end{align*} and so~\eqref{ruzsa-3} is a consequence of~\Cref{cond-dist-fact}. Once again the second form of the result is immediate from the definition of $\dist{Y}{Z}$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 and the Kaimanovich-Vershik-Madiman inequality
